title: Checks an agent cannot weaken
bridge: A check an agent cannot weaken is like a Playwright suite owned by another team, in a repo you cannot push to. Your PR must pass it, and you cannot edit it. Except the 'cannot' must come from GitHub permissions and a ruleset. An agent that wants a green check tries the cheapest edit, and the test is often the cheapest one.
intro: An agent is judged by checks: tests, lint, coverage and an approval. Sooner or later it will turn a check green by changing the check instead of the code. This lesson shows the four checks that close that path and where each one must live. It also shows what each does when it fires: block, warn or reject.

picture.caption: Four places say no to a weakened check, from inside the VM to the merge button.

nodes.label: Nova or a routine (in the VM)

tries to push a change to .github/workflows; GitHub refuses the push
edits a test with sed in Bash, which the hook does not see, and opens the PR

reads the warnings and approves the head commit
passes only because the approver is outside the requester set

sections.h: A green build that proves nothing
p: Picture the FE CI fixer routine from G5. frontend-ci went red on main because one unit test fails. The routine has three ways to make it green. It can fix the code, add it.skip to the test, or delete the failing expect() line.
All three turn CI green. Only the first one fixes anything. The other two make the check prove less, and the build looks healthy while the bug ships.

This is called reward hacking. A system judged by a score finds a cheaper way to raise the score than doing the task. Models do it with tests, because a test is often the cheapest thing to change. We do not argue with it in the prompt. We arrange the checks so the cheap path does not work.

callout.text: Agents never change the checks they are judged by. The rest of this lesson is how infrastructure, not a prompt, holds that rule.

p: Ask three questions about any check an agent is judged by. Where does its code live? Who may change its rules? What does it read?

Its code must live where the agent cannot write. Our checks live in RhinoHealth/ai-agents and ship in the ai-agents-checks image, pinned by digest. fcp calls them from a workflow pinned by commit SHA. The agent's token covers one repo, fcp, so it cannot reach the check's code.

Its rules must change only through a person. The fcp ruleset lists the check as required, and agent apps have no bypass. Changing the list or the code is a PR that one person approves, and that person is never the agent.
It must read facts, not claims. independent-approval reads reviews and commits from the GitHub API, and locked-checks reads the diff. Neither trusts a sentence the agent wrote, like 'all tests pass'.

callout.text: A coverage threshold in fcp's own config, read by fcp's own CI, fails the first question: the agent can edit it. That is why cloud/.coveragerc is on the locked list.

sections.h: Four layers, from the VM to the merge button
p: The first layer is a hook in the VM (G3-21). A PreToolUse hook refuses an Edit or Write on a protected path and records the refusal. The agent gets a calm reason and an alternative at once, before it wastes an hour.

The hook is not enough on its own. It matches the Edit and Write tools, so a Bash command like sed -i changes a file without the hook seeing it. That is why the next layers look at the result, not at the tool call.

The second layer is the token. The rhino-ai-agents App has no workflows permission, so GitHub refuses any push that changes .github/workflows (lesson p11-2). The third layer is the required checks, which read the PR's final diff. The fourth is the ruleset: no merge until every required check passes and one independent person approves.

callout.text: One file feeds both the hook and the check: ai-agents/settings/protected-paths.yaml, one block per repo. So the VM and GitHub never disagree about what is locked.

sections.h: Independent approval: a person outside the change
p: GitHub stops an author approving their own PR. On an agent PR the author is the bot, so the person who asked for the work could approve it alone. That breaks our rule: exactly one approval, never by the requester.

The independent-approval check (G0-09) builds a requester set. The PR author is in it, plus the login on the Requested-by: line the orchestrator writes into the PR body. Anyone who pushed a commit or edited the body joins it too.

Then it looks for an APPROVED review from a person outside that set. The review must be on the head commit, the PR's latest commit. An agent PR with no Requested-by: line fails. That is failing closed: when the input a check needs is missing, it fails instead of passing.
Byte's fix mode gets the same rule in G2-05. A fix commit carries a Requested-by: trailer. So main needs an approval from someone other than the person who asked for the fix.
Not every finding should stop a PR. People edit tests for good reasons, like a renamed field or a changed screen. So each check gives one of three answers, depending on who wrote the PR.

locked-checks blocks (G0-18). An agent PR that edits CI, lint, type or test config fails, and a person can take the PR over. Human PRs pass straight through. weakened-tests warns (G0-19) on every PR, from people and agents. It adds an annotation, a note GitHub shows on a line of the diff, and never fails.

The false-heal check rejects (G5-14). A false heal is a change that turns a check green by weakening it. For Nova a finding is a flag in the PR, because a person reads every Nova PR. For a routine, which runs unattended, any finding rejects the run. It also moves the routine one step back on its trust ladder (shadow, drafts to the owner, normal).
sections.because: We write the three answers as one small function, so who gets blocked, warned or rejected becomes a rule you can test.

notes.text: Lab code: the shape of the rule, not a file from the tickets.
Three kinds of author. A routine runs unattended; Nova and people have a person reading the PR.
Inputs: who wrote it, whether a locked path changed, and the false-heal findings from the next section.
Agents that touch a locked path are blocked first, whatever else is true. People are not limited here.
No findings: the PR passes these checks and goes on to review.
A routine with any finding is rejected. Nobody reads its PR before the run ends, so the check decides.
Everyone else gets a warning on the diff. The one reviewer decides if the test edit was fair.

sections.h: Reading a diff for a weaker test
p: The weakened-test and false-heal checks read the patch: the unified diff of one file. A line starting with + was added, a line starting with - was removed. The +++ and --- lines at the top are file headers, not changes.

Three signs matter. An added skip or .only. More assertions removed than added in a test file. A threshold line whose number moved the loose way. The code below is a small version of G0-19 and G5-14 that you build in the lab.
sections.because: We read only the changed lines, because the question is what this PR did to the checks, not what the file says.

notes.text: Which paths count as tests: tests/, test/, e2e/, *.test.ts(x), *.spec.ts(x) and Python test_*.py.
Assertion lines: expect( for Vitest and Playwright, assert for pytest and node:assert, self.assert... for unittest.
A skip or a focus. .only is here too: it makes every other test in the file stop running.
A threshold: a key like fail_under, retries or timeout, then = or :, then a number captured in group 2.
Keep only + and - lines, and drop the +++ and --- headers that also start with those signs.
Added lines, with the sign cut off. Line 10 does the same for removed lines.
Every added line that skips or focuses a test becomes a finding, in any file.
In test files only: removed assertions minus added ones. A rewritten assertion counts zero.
Only a net loss is reported, with the number lost.
Each threshold that changed, as key, old value, new value. The next section explains these two helpers.
An empty list means no false heal was found.

p: A threshold can move two ways, and only one is a weakening. A lower fail-under accepts less coverage, so lower is looser. More retries or a longer timeout lets a flaky test pass by luck, so higher is looser.

So the check pairs a removed threshold line with an added line for the same key. Then it asks which way the number moved. Raising fail_under from 70 to 85 makes the check stricter and gives no finding.
sections.because: We compare old and new values per key, because 'the number changed' alone would also flag every tightening.

notes.text: loosened answers one question for one key: did this change make the check easier to pass?
Keys with fail in the name (fail_under, fail-under): a smaller number is looser. Others: a bigger number is looser.
thresholdChanges returns [key, old, new] for each key that appears on a removed and an added line.
Run the THRESHOLD pattern on each removed line; skip lines that hold no threshold.
Find an added line with the same key, ignoring case. That pair is one change of one threshold.
Numbers come out of the regex as strings, so Number() turns them into numbers before comparing.

p: These checks count and compare. They cannot judge meaning. Change expect(total).toBe(3) to expect(total).toBeTruthy() and the count of assertions stays the same, so nothing fires.

That is why the checks are never alone. The one reviewer reads the diff. In G4, Nova writes the QA checks as failing tests before the code. The plan's block in the PR body adds those files to the locked list. A nightly mutation report (G7-35) plants small bugs in the code and shows the tests that still pass.
Calibrate a warning before you trust it. G0-19 runs over the last 50 merged fcp PRs first. It may raise at most one false alarm per ten PRs, or the noisy pattern goes.

callout.text: When a warning fires on your own PR, answer it in the description. 'The assertion moved to a helper in format.test.ts' takes one line and saves the reviewer ten minutes.

quiz.q: Nova's PreToolUse hook refuses edits to cloud/.coveragerc. Why do we still need the locked-checks required check?

options.text: Because hooks only run on people's laptops, not in the VM
options.why: The harness hooks run in the VM; G3-21 puts them in nova-worker.

options.text: Because sed -i in Bash changes the file without an Edit or Write call, and the check reads the final diff
options.why: The hook sees tool calls; the check sees the result. Together they cover both.

options.text: Because the hook only warns and never refuses
options.why: The hook denies with a reason. It is a real refusal, but only for the tool calls it matches.

quiz.q: A routine's PR turns CI green by adding it.skip to the failing test. What happens?

options.text: The run is rejected as a false heal, and the routine moves one step back on its trust ladder
options.why: Routines run unattended, so any false-heal finding rejects the run (G5-14).

options.text: The PR gets a warning annotation and waits for review
options.why: That is the answer for a person's or Nova's PR. A routine has nobody reading it first.

options.text: Nothing: the build is green, so the PR is fine
options.why: A green build after a new skip proves less than before. That is exactly the false heal the check exists for.

quiz.q: Where must the code of a check that judges agent PRs in fcp live?

options.text: In fcp's .github/workflows, so fcp's team can read it
options.why: fcp is the one repo the agent's token covers. Only the thin caller lives there; the logic must not.

options.text: In the agent's prompt, as a list of files it must not edit
options.why: A prompt is guidance. Text in a ticket can argue with it; a required check cannot be argued with.

options.text: In RhinoHealth/ai-agents, shipped as an image pinned by digest, called from fcp by a workflow pinned by SHA
options.why: The agent cannot write there, and fcp only changes the pin through a reviewed PR.

recall: From p11-2: which GitHub App permission does the broker never request, and what does GitHub then refuse?
From p2-4: how does a ruleset treat a required check whose job was skipped?

words.plain: Raising a score a cheaper way than doing the task, for example by editing the test that gives the score.
A required check that fails an agent PR changing CI, lint, type or test config, or its plan's QA checks.
ai-agents/settings/protected-paths.yaml: one list per repo that both the VM hook and the locked-checks check read.
A test edit that makes the test easier to pass: a removed assertion, a new skip, a looser threshold.
A change that makes a red check green by weakening the check instead of fixing the code.
When the input a check needs is missing, the check fails instead of passing.
The people who are part of a change: the author, the Requested-by login, commit authors and body editors.

tickets.why: The independent-approval check: the requester set, approvals on the head commit only, and failing closed.
The locked-checks check: code outside fcp, one protected-paths file, and a block for agent PRs only.
The weakened-tests check: read the patch, warn on every PR, calibrate on 50 merged PRs first.
The false-heal check: the same signs plus the charter rules, and a reject for routines.

remember: A check an agent cannot weaken lives outside the repo it writes, changes only through a person, and reads facts, not claims.
